theme: Honest numbers: reading metrics without fooling yourself, AI costs, and WhatsApp's new pricing

questions.concept: Designing for first-time, low-literacy internet users
questions.question: You're asked to design a payments app for first-time smartphone users in rural India, many with limited reading ability. Which design direction best fits these users?
options: Voice prompts in the local language, icon-led flows and a confirm screen showing the payee's photo
A dense dashboard of spending charts and categories so users see everything in one place
A text-heavy tutorial at sign-up that explains every feature before first use
An English-first interface with a translate button available on every screen
questions.explanation: The binding constraint is literacy and digital familiarity, not feature breadth. Voice in the user's language, recognisable icons and a visual confirmation (photo, name read aloud) reduce reading load and the fear of sending money to the wrong person. Strong product-sense answers let the user's constraint drive the design rather than adding more screens or text.
rationales: Correct. It removes reading as a requirement and adds trust cues at the riskiest moment (confirming the payee).
Dense data views demand literacy and numeracy these users may lack; it serves power users, not this segment.
A long text tutorial front-loads exactly the skill (reading) the user struggles with, so most will skip or abandon it.
English-first with translation still assumes reading ability; translation doesn't fix low literacy.
questions.interview_tip: State the segment's defining constraint out loud ('can't rely on reading') and show each solution flows from it. Interviewers reward designs that handle trust and error-prevention for novice users.

questions.concept: Curb-cut effect of designing for edge users
questions.question: A maps team adds step-free routes for wheelchair users. Soon parents with strollers and travellers with luggage use it heavily too. What product principle does this illustrate?
options: Solving well for a constrained group often creates a better product for many others
Niche segments should be avoided because their features get hijacked by others
Accessibility features should be hidden to avoid confusing mainstream users
Feature usage by unintended users means the original segment was mis-chosen
questions.explanation: This is the 'curb-cut effect': ramps built for wheelchairs help strollers, carts and cyclists. Designing deeply for a user with a hard constraint often surfaces a latent need shared by a wider group. It's a strong argument for starting with a sharply defined segment in product-sense interviews.
rationales: Correct. Designing for the extreme user exposed a broader need (avoid stairs) that many people share.
Broader adoption is a benefit, not a hijack; it increases the feature's value and justification.
Hiding it would deny value to both the core and adjacent users who clearly want it.
The core segment was served well; extra adopters show the need was wider, not that the choice was wrong.
questions.interview_tip: When you pick a narrow segment, mention that strong solutions for it may generalise. It shows you can focus without losing sight of reach.

questions.concept: Pre-mortem on a proposed solution's failure modes
questions.question: Your product-sense answer proposes 'neighbourhood groups' in a social app so neighbours can share recommendations. You have 5 minutes left. What should you do to strengthen the answer most?
options: Name key risks such as misuse for profiling or harassment and how you'd mitigate them
Add three more features to the groups idea to show breadth of thinking
Recap the full answer from the beginning so the interviewer remembers it
Describe the tech stack and database design needed to build the groups
questions.explanation: Strong product-sense answers close by stress-testing the chosen solution: what could go wrong, for whom, and how you'd mitigate it. Local groups carry real risks (racial profiling, harassment, misinformation) that a senior PM would anticipate. Showing trade-off awareness is worth more than extra features at the end.
rationales: Correct. Anticipating downsides and mitigations signals judgement and maturity, which top-tier loops weigh heavily.
More features dilutes focus; interviewers want depth on one solution, not a longer list.
A full recap uses scarce time without adding new signal; a crisp one-line summary would do.
Implementation details are out of scope for product sense and don't show product judgement.
questions.interview_tip: Reserve the last minutes for 'risks and how I'd measure success'. Meta and Google interviewers explicitly look for trade-off and harm awareness.

questions.question: A photo-editing app asks for camera, location, contacts and notification permissions on the first screen, and opt-in rates are poor. What's the best fix?
options: Ask for each permission at the moment a feature needs it, with a short reason
Bundle all permissions into one combined prompt so users tap only once
Block app use until users grant every permission on the first screen
Move the requests to a settings page that users can visit when they choose
questions.explanation: Users grant permissions when they understand why, and context makes the reason obvious. Requesting the camera when the user taps 'take photo', with a one-line rationale, raises opt-in and trust. Front-loading every request before the user has seen any value triggers reflexive denial.
rationales: Correct. Contextual, just-in-time requests tie the permission to a visible benefit, raising grant rates.
Operating systems don't allow true bundling, and it still asks before the user sees value.
Forcing permissions creates resentment and abandonment; app stores also discourage it.
Burying requests in settings means most users never grant them, so features silently fail.
questions.interview_tip: In onboarding questions, talk about 'asking at the moment of value'. It shows you think about trust and sequencing, not just screens.

questions.concept: Segmenting a metric drop by app version
questions.question: Checkout conversion fell 6% overnight. Web is flat, iOS is flat, and the whole drop is on Android. What is the most useful next cut?
options: Split Android conversion by app version to see if the latest release is the cause
Survey a sample of Android users about their recent checkout experience
Compare this week's conversion with the same week last year
Check whether marketing spend on Android acquisition campaigns changed
questions.explanation: A sudden, platform-specific drop points to something that shipped or broke on that platform. Cutting by app version quickly tests whether the new release is responsible; if only the newest version is down, you've localised the bug. Good root-causing narrows the space with the cheapest, most discriminating cut first.
rationales: Correct. An overnight drop isolated to one platform is most often a release or client bug; version split confirms it fast.
Surveys are slow and noisy; they won't localise an overnight technical drop.
Year-over-year helps for seasonality, but an overnight single-platform drop isn't seasonal.
Spend changes shift traffic mix gradually; they don't usually cause an overnight conversion cliff on one platform.
questions.interview_tip: Narrate your funnel of hypotheses: internal (release, tracking) before external (seasonality, competitors). Interviewers look for structured, fast elimination.

questions.concept: Ratio metric moved by its denominator
questions.question: Notification click-through rate jumped from 4% to 7% after a change. Total clicks are unchanged. What most likely happened?
options: Fewer notifications were sent, so the same clicks divided by a smaller base
Users found the new notification copy far more compelling to open
The tracking pipeline started double-counting notification opens
More new users joined, and new users always click more often
questions.explanation: A ratio can move because the numerator changes or because the denominator does. With clicks flat and CTR up, sends (the denominator) must have dropped. Always check both components before celebrating a ratio; here, engagement didn't actually grow.
rationales: Correct. Flat clicks with a higher rate means the base shrank; the 'win' is arithmetic, not engagement.
Better copy would raise clicks, but clicks didn't move.
Double-counting would inflate clicks, which are flat.
A user-mix shift could raise CTR, but you'd see clicks grow too; and 'always' is unsupported.
questions.interview_tip: Whenever a ratio moves, say 'let me check the numerator and denominator separately'. It's a quick signal of analytical rigour.

questions.question: Data shows users who create a playlist retain at twice the rate of those who don't. A stakeholder wants to force every new user to create one. What's the best response?
options: Engaged users self-select into playlists; test whether prompting causes the lift
Agree, because a 2x retention gap is large enough to act on immediately
Ignore the data, since retention is driven mostly by content quality
Remove playlists for half of users to measure how much retention falls
questions.explanation: Correlation between a feature and retention is often selection: already-committed users do more things. Forcing the behaviour may not move retention and can add friction. The right move is an experiment (e.g., a gentle playlist prompt vs control) to estimate the causal effect before committing.
rationales: Correct. It names the bias and proposes a causal test that is cheap and ethical.
Acting on correlation risks adding friction for no gain; the 2x may be entirely selection.
Dismissing the data throws away a useful hypothesis worth testing.
Taking away an existing feature harms users and measures something different from a prompt.
questions.interview_tip: Say 'that's correlation; engaged users self-select' and propose the experiment. Meta's analytical rounds probe exactly this 'aha moment' trap.

questions.question: An Indian e-commerce app's orders are down 30% week-over-week, right after the Diwali sale week. What should you check first?
options: Compare with the same post-festival week last year to account for seasonality
Escalate an incident, since a 30% drop is always a critical outage
Launch an emergency discount to recover the lost order volume
Ask engineering to audit every service deployed in the last week
questions.explanation: Comparing against a sale week inflates the baseline; post-festival dips are normal. A year-over-year or same-period comparison separates seasonality from a real problem. Only if the dip is unusual versus past years should you dig into incidents.
rationales: Correct. The right baseline removes the predictable festival spike before you investigate.
A drop after a peak isn't automatically an outage; escalating wastes time and erodes trust.
Discounting reacts to a possibly normal pattern and burns margin.
An engineering audit is premature until the drop is shown to be abnormal.
questions.interview_tip: Mention external/seasonal factors early in root-cause questions. It shows you won't chase phantom problems.

questions.question: An A/B test on 50 million users shows a 0.02% lift in session length with p < 0.001. The change adds ongoing maintenance cost. What's the right read?
options: The effect is real but likely too small to justify the cost; weigh impact, not just p
Ship it, because p < 0.001 means the result is highly important
Discard it, because tiny effects at huge sample sizes are always false positives
Re-run with fewer users so the p-value becomes more trustworthy
questions.explanation: With huge samples, tiny effects become statistically significant. Significance says the effect is probably not zero; it says nothing about whether it matters. Decide by comparing the effect size (and its confidence interval) with the cost and the minimum effect worth shipping.
rationales: Correct. It separates 'is it real' from 'is it worth it' and ties the decision to cost.
A small p-value signals confidence, not magnitude or business value.
Large samples don't make results false; they make small real effects detectable.
Fewer users lowers power; it doesn't make a result more trustworthy.
questions.interview_tip: Talk about effect size and confidence intervals, not only p-values. Interviewers use this to separate stats-literate PMs from dashboard readers.

questions.question: You're testing a new search ranking for a shopping app. Randomizing by session would let the same user see different rankings across visits. Why is user-level randomization usually better here?
options: It keeps each user's experience consistent and avoids carryover between variants
It always produces more statistical power than session-level randomization
It is the only unit analytics tools are able to log correctly
It removes the need for guardrail metrics in the experiment
questions.explanation: When the treatment can affect later behaviour (learning where items appear, cart contents), session-level splits leak: one user sees both variants and outcomes blend. User-level randomization keeps exposure consistent and lets you measure user outcomes like conversion and retention. The trade-off is fewer independent units, so power can be lower.
rationales: Correct. Consistency and no cross-variant contamination make user-level the safer choice for experiences users learn.
Session-level actually has more units and often more power; user-level trades some power for validity.
Tools can log sessions fine; the choice is about validity, not logging.
Guardrails are still needed regardless of the randomization unit.
questions.interview_tip: Mention randomization unit (user, session, device, cluster) proactively in A/B design answers. It's a common senior-level differentiator.

questions.question: An AI assistant has 2 million daily active users, each sending 5 queries a day. Each query uses about 1,500 tokens (input plus output), and blended pricing is $2 per million tokens. Roughly what is the monthly inference bill?
options: About $90,000
About $9 million
About $27 million
questions.explanation: Queries per day = 2M x 5 = 10M. Tokens per day = 10M x 1,500 = 15 billion. Per month (30 days) = 450 billion tokens = 450,000 million. At $2 per million, cost = 450,000 x $2 = $900,000. Laying out units at every step prevents order-of-magnitude slips.
rationales: Correct. 10M queries/day x 1,500 tokens x 30 days = 450B tokens; 450,000 x $2 = $0.9M.
This is off by 10x, typically from dropping a zero when converting billions of tokens to millions.
This is 10x too high, a common slip when multiplying tokens by 30 days twice or mis-scaling units.
This likely multiplies by 30 twice or confuses per-thousand with per-million pricing.
questions.interview_tip: In AI PM interviews, show the cost chain: users -> queries -> tokens -> price. Then mention levers (caching, routing, shorter prompts).

questions.question: A short-video app has 300 million daily active users. About 2% upload one video a day, and videos average 30 seconds. Roughly how many hours of video are uploaded per day?
options: About 50,000 hours
About 5,000 hours
About 500,000 hours
About 5 million hours
questions.explanation: Uploaders = 300M x 2% = 6M videos a day. Seconds = 6M x 30 = 180M seconds. Hours = 180M / 3,600 = 50,000 hours. This kind of figure drives storage, moderation and transcoding capacity planning.
rationales: Correct. 6M uploads x 30 s = 180M s, divided by 3,600 = 50,000 hours.
10x too low, usually from using 0.2% instead of 2% uploaders.
10x too high, often from dividing by 360 instead of 3,600 seconds per hour.
100x too high; it treats too many users as uploaders or forgets to convert seconds to hours.
questions.interview_tip: State assumptions, compute cleanly, then sanity-check against something known. Then say what the number is used for (e.g., moderation staffing).

questions.question: A B2B SaaS tool has one $50/month plan. Small teams say it's too expensive, and enterprises want SSO and audit logs. What pricing move best captures both?
options: Introduce tiers: a cheaper basic plan and an enterprise tier with SSO and audit logs
Cut the single price to $30 so more small teams can afford it
Raise the single price to $80 and add SSO for everyone
Offer custom quotes to every customer instead of a public price
questions.explanation: Versioning lets customers self-select by willingness to pay. A basic tier opens the price-sensitive segment, while an enterprise tier charges for features (SSO, audit) that large buyers value highly and small teams don't need. One price leaves money on the table at both ends.
rationales: Correct. Tiers segment customers by value and capture surplus from enterprises without losing small teams.
A blanket cut gives a discount to enterprises who would pay more.
A higher single price pushes out small teams and bundles features they don't value.
Custom quotes for everyone adds sales cost and friction for small self-serve buyers.
questions.interview_tip: In pricing questions, name the segments and their willingness to pay, then design fences (features) between tiers.

questions.concept: Data network effects as an AI moat
questions.question: A startup pitches: 'More users give us more data, which makes our AI better, so we'll have an unbeatable moat.' What's the strongest critique?
options: Data advantages often plateau and can be matched by foundation models, so the loop may be weak
Data never improves AI products, so the claim has no basis at all
Network effects only exist in social networks, never in AI products
The moat is fine; the only risk is that servers become too expensive
questions.explanation: Data loops can help, but the marginal value of extra data usually diminishes, and strong general-purpose models may close the gap without your data. A durable moat needs proprietary data that keeps improving outcomes users notice, plus other advantages (workflow, distribution). Challenging 'data moat' claims is a classic AI-strategy test.
rationales: Correct. It identifies diminishing returns and commoditisation by foundation models as the key weaknesses.
Overstated; data can improve products, the question is whether the advantage is durable.
Data network effects can exist outside social apps; the question is their strength.
Cost matters, but it misses the core strategic flaw in the moat argument.
questions.interview_tip: When asked about AI moats, separate 'data helps' from 'data defends'. Mention distribution, workflow lock-in and proprietary feedback loops.

questions.concept: Choosing a beachhead segment for market entry
questions.question: A new expense-management app wants to enter a crowded market. Which entry approach is usually strongest?
options: Win a narrow segment with a sharp, unmet need, then expand from that foothold
Launch to every company size at once to maximise the addressable market
Match every feature of the market leader before launching anything
Compete mainly on the lowest price across all customer segments
questions.explanation: A beachhead is a focused segment where you can be clearly better and win word-of-mouth quickly. Dominating it builds references and revenue to expand into adjacent segments. Going broad against incumbents spreads resources thin.
rationales: Correct. Focus lets a newcomer be meaningfully better for someone, which is how entrants win.
Going broad against established players spreads a small team too thin to win anywhere.
Feature parity takes years and still gives users no reason to switch.
Pure price competition is easy to match and erodes the business.
questions.interview_tip: In market-entry questions, name the beachhead and why you can win it, then the expansion path.

questions.question: Engineers say tech debt is slowing every release, but sales wants new features. What's the most effective way to handle this?
options: Reserve a fixed share of capacity for debt tied to measurable delivery gains
Pause all features for a quarter to clear the entire backlog of debt
Ignore debt until it causes a visible outage, then fix it
Let engineers work on debt only during weekends and hackathons
questions.explanation: Sustained, explicit capacity (often 15-25%) for debt keeps velocity healthy without stopping roadmap delivery. Tying debt work to outcomes like cycle time or incident rate makes the trade-off visible to stakeholders. All-or-nothing approaches either stall the business or let quality decay.
rationales: Correct. A standing allocation with measurable benefits balances short-term features and long-term speed.
A full freeze stalls customer value and is hard to justify to the business.
Waiting for outages means paying debt at the worst time, with customer impact.
Off-hours work is unsustainable and signals debt isn't real work.
questions.interview_tip: Frame tech debt in business terms (speed, reliability). Interviewers want to see you can negotiate both sides.

questions.question: Why do strong PRDs include an explicit 'Non-goals' section?
options: To state what's out of scope so the team avoids creep and debate later
To list features that were rejected forever and must never be built
To record the risks that could cause the project to fail
To describe the metrics the team will deliberately not track
questions.explanation: Non-goals make scope boundaries explicit: what this version won't do. That prevents scope creep, aligns stakeholders early and speeds up decisions. They're about this project, not permanent bans.
rationales: Correct. Clear non-goals align expectations and protect scope.
Non-goals are for this release; they can be revisited later.
Risks belong in a separate risks section.
Metrics you won't track isn't what non-goals are for.
questions.interview_tip: When describing how you write specs, mention goals and non-goals. It signals you manage scope proactively.

questions.question: Your launch depends on a payments-team API that's two weeks late, and it sits on the critical path. What should you do first?
options: Raise it now, assess re-sequencing or a stub, and agree a new date or scope with stakeholders
Wait quietly, since the payments team may still catch up before launch
Ask your engineers to build their own payments system in parallel
Cancel the launch and restart planning from scratch next quarter
questions.explanation: A late critical-path dependency moves the launch unless you act. Surface it early, explore mitigations (re-order work, build against a mock, cut scope), and reset expectations transparently. Hiding slips or over-reacting both damage trust.
rationales: Correct. Early transparency plus concrete mitigations is how strong PMs handle dependency risk.
Hoping it resolves leaves stakeholders surprised later.
Duplicating a payments system is costly, risky and wastes effort.
Cancelling is premature when mitigations exist.
questions.interview_tip: Show you track the critical path and communicate slips early. 'No surprises' is a common bar for senior PMs.

questions.concept: Deciding with incomplete data on a reversible choice
questions.question: In a behavioural round you're asked about deciding without enough data. Which story best shows good judgement?
options: You saw the choice was reversible, set a deadline, decided with 70% of the data, and defined a rollback signal
You delayed the decision for six weeks until every stakeholder agreed
You asked your manager to decide so the risk wasn't on you
You picked the option you liked and didn't revisit it afterwards
questions.explanation: Strong answers separate one-way doors (hard to reverse, decide carefully) from two-way doors (reversible, decide fast). Acting on enough data, with an explicit signal for reversing, shows bias for action without recklessness. Amazon's Leadership Principles explicitly reward this.
rationales: Correct. It shows calibrated speed, risk awareness and a learning loop.
Waiting for full consensus on a reversible call wastes time and signals low ownership.
Pushing the decision up avoids ownership, a red flag in behavioural rounds.
Deciding without a check-in shows no learning loop or risk thinking.
questions.interview_tip: Use the 'one-way vs two-way door' framing and give the metric you watched afterwards. It maps directly to Amazon's 'Bias for Action'.

questions.concept: Delivering bad news to leadership early
questions.question: You realise mid-quarter your team will miss a committed goal. Which approach shows the strongest ownership?
options: Tell leadership now with the cause, the revised forecast and a recovery plan
Wait until the quarterly review in case the numbers recover by then
Reframe the goal in the review so the miss looks like a different success
Inform leadership but explain that the miss was caused by another team
questions.explanation: Leaders want no surprises. Raising a miss early, with root cause, a realistic forecast and options, gives them time to adjust and builds trust. Hiding, spinning or blaming erodes credibility even if the eventual outcome is the same.
rationales: Correct. Early, owned communication with a plan is what 'earn trust' looks like.
Waiting removes leadership's chance to help and makes the miss a surprise.
Spin is usually detected and damages credibility.
Blaming others signals low ownership, even if dependencies contributed.
questions.interview_tip: In 'tell me about a failure' stories, show you raised it early and what you changed. Interviewers listen for ownership, not perfection.

questions.concept: Saying no to a large customer's one-off request
questions.question: Your biggest enterprise customer demands a custom feature only they would use, threatening to churn. How should you respond?
options: Dig into the underlying need, look for a general solution, and be clear on what you won't build
Build it right away because losing the biggest customer is not an option
Decline immediately because custom features are always a bad idea
Hand it to sales so product isn't involved in the negotiation
questions.explanation: Customer obsession means solving the customer's real problem, not executing every request. Understanding the job behind the ask often reveals a solution that serves many customers; where you can't, saying no clearly with reasons preserves trust. Pure yes or pure no both skip the discovery.
rationales: Correct. It balances customer value with product coherence through discovery and clear communication.
One-off builds create long-term maintenance burden and turn the product into a services shop.
A reflexive no ignores a possible real need and may lose the customer unnecessarily.
Product owns the trade-off; abdicating it to sales loses context and control.
questions.interview_tip: Show the 'why behind the ask' step and how you communicated the decision. It signals both customer empathy and product discipline.

questions.question: After a safety update, your AI assistant's harmful-output rate drops, but support tickets about 'it won't answer normal questions' rise. What metric should you add?
options: False-refusal rate on a set of benign prompts that should be answered
Average response length across all conversations
Total number of safety rules in the system prompt
Percentage of users who have read the content policy
questions.explanation: Safety tuning has two errors: harmful answers (missed) and benign requests refused (over-blocking). Measuring only the first pushes the model toward refusing too much, hurting helpfulness. A benign eval set with a false-refusal rate makes the trade-off visible.
rationales: Correct. It directly measures the helpfulness cost of safety changes.
Response length doesn't capture whether legitimate questions get refused.
Rule count is an input, not an outcome measure.
Policy readership doesn't tell you whether the model refuses benign requests.
questions.interview_tip: Frame AI safety as a precision/recall trade-off with metrics for both sides. It shows you understand helpfulness and harmlessness together.

questions.question: A help-centre search returns nothing for 'can't log in' because articles say 'sign-in issues'. What technique best fixes this?
options: Embedding-based semantic search that matches by meaning, not exact words
Adding more keywords to each article's title manually
Raising the LLM temperature so results become more creative
Sorting results by article publish date instead of relevance
questions.explanation: Embeddings map text to vectors so semantically similar phrases sit close together, even with different words. Semantic search retrieves 'sign-in issues' for 'can't log in'. It's the retrieval foundation of most RAG systems.
rationales: Correct. Embeddings capture meaning, solving vocabulary mismatch.
Manual keywords help a little but can't anticipate every phrasing.
Temperature affects generation randomness, not retrieval.
Date sorting doesn't fix the vocabulary mismatch.
questions.interview_tip: Explain embeddings in one plain sentence. AI PM interviews often check you can describe retrieval without jargon.

questions.question: An AI system classifies insurance claims. It is very accurate when confident but makes costly errors when unsure. What's the best product design?
options: Auto-process high-confidence claims and route low-confidence ones to human reviewers
Send every claim to humans, since the model sometimes makes errors
Auto-process every claim, since accuracy is high on average
Ask the model to explain each decision instead of reviewing any
questions.explanation: A confidence threshold lets automation handle the easy majority while humans handle ambiguous cases. You tune the threshold by weighing review cost against error cost. This captures most of the efficiency while containing risk.
rationales: Correct. It allocates human effort where the model is weakest.
Full human review throws away the automation value.
Average accuracy hides the costly low-confidence errors.
Explanations don't prevent errors and can sound convincing even when wrong.
questions.interview_tip: Mention calibration and how you'd set the threshold from costs. It shows practical AI deployment thinking.

questions.concept: Offline eval gains not translating online
questions.question: A new model scores 8 points higher on your offline eval set, but in the A/B test user satisfaction is flat. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The eval set no longer reflects what real users ask, so offline gains miss real usage
A/B tests can't measure AI quality, so the online result should be ignored
The 8-point gain is too large to be real, so the eval must have a bug
Users can't notice quality differences, so model improvements never matter
questions.explanation: Offline evals are proxies. If the set drifts from real traffic, or measures things users don't value, gains won't show up online. The fix is refreshing the eval set from production samples and checking which dimensions correlate with satisfaction.
rationales: Correct. Eval-to-reality mismatch is the most common reason offline wins don't move online metrics.
Online tests are the ground truth for user impact; ignore them at your peril.
Large gains can be real; the issue is relevance, not size.
Users do notice quality; the eval just measured the wrong thing.
questions.interview_tip: Say you'd keep evals grounded in production traffic and validate them against online metrics. It shows mature AI-eval thinking.

questions.question: Every request to your AI agent includes the same 20,000-token system prompt and tool definitions. Which change most directly cuts cost and latency?
options: Use prompt caching so the shared prefix is processed once and reused
Switch to a larger model so it reads the long prompt more efficiently
Raise max output tokens so each request does more work at once
Move the system prompt to the end of the user message
questions.explanation: Prompt caching stores the processed form of a repeated prefix, so later calls skip recomputing it, cutting input cost and time to first token. It works best when stable content (system prompt, tools, documents) comes first. Many providers bill cached input tokens at a large discount.
rationales: Correct. Caching the stable prefix is the direct lever for repeated long context.
Larger models are usually slower and pricier per token.
More output tokens increases cost and latency.
Moving stable content later breaks the shared prefix, making caching impossible.
questions.interview_tip: When discussing AI cost, list levers: caching, routing, prompt trimming, batching. Knowing caching signals hands-on experience.

questions.question: An API returns a user's order history, which can have thousands of items, and new orders arrive constantly. Why prefer cursor-based pagination over page numbers?
options: Cursors give stable results as new items arrive, avoiding skipped or duplicated rows
Cursors let clients download the entire history in one single response
Page numbers are not supported by any modern database system
Cursors remove the need for authentication on each request
questions.explanation: With page numbers (offset), inserting new items shifts everything, so users can see duplicates or miss items between pages. A cursor marks a position (e.g., last item's ID) so the next page continues from there. Cursors also scale better on large tables.
rationales: Correct. Cursors anchor to a position, so concurrent inserts don't shift pages.
Pagination's purpose is to split results, not return all at once.
Offset pagination is widely supported; it just has drawbacks.
Pagination and authentication are unrelated.
questions.interview_tip: In technical rounds, tie API choices to user-visible problems ('duplicates in the feed'). That's what interviewers want from PMs.

questions.concept: Encryption in transit vs at rest
questions.question: Your security review asks whether customer data is encrypted 'in transit' and 'at rest'. What's the difference?
options: In transit protects data moving over networks; at rest protects data stored on disks
In transit covers mobile apps; at rest covers websites
In transit is for passwords only; at rest is for all other data
They are two names for the same TLS protection
questions.explanation: Encryption in transit (e.g., TLS) protects data as it travels between client and server or between services. Encryption at rest protects stored data (databases, backups) if disks or snapshots are accessed. Security reviews expect both.
rationales: Correct. They cover different threat moments: interception vs stolen storage.
Both apply to any platform; the split is by data state, not app type.
Both apply to all sensitive data, not just passwords.
TLS covers transit only; at-rest needs storage-level encryption.
questions.interview_tip: Know the basics of data protection when discussing B2B or enterprise products; security questions often come up in deals.

questions.question: A consumer app loses 85% of new users within a week. The CEO wants to double the ad budget. What's the best advice?
options: Improve early retention first, since paid users will mostly churn just as fast
Double spend now, since more users means more revenue regardless
Switch all spend to influencer marketing to attract better users
Cut onboarding to one screen so users sign up faster
questions.explanation: This is the leaky-bucket problem: pouring more users into a product that can't retain them wastes acquisition spend. Fixing early retention raises the lifetime value of every acquired user, making growth spend efficient. Scale acquisition once retention curves flatten at a healthy level.
rationales: Correct. Retention multiplies the value of every acquisition dollar.
More users who churn quickly rarely pay back their acquisition cost.
A channel switch may help slightly but doesn't fix the product's retention.
Faster signup increases top-of-funnel but doesn't address week-one churn.
questions.interview_tip: Mention the leaky bucket and LTV/CAC when spend comes up. It signals you think about sustainable growth.

questions.question: From 1 October 2026, WhatsApp Business Platform pricing changed for customer-service conversations. What is the new rule?
options: Service messages are free up to 1,000 per business number per month, then charged
All service messages became chargeable from the very first reply
Customers now pay a small fee to receive messages from businesses
The 24-hour customer-service window was removed entirely
questions.explanation: From 1 October 2026, service messages (replies within the customer-service window) are free for the first 1,000 delivered per business phone number each month; beyond that they're charged. Utility templates sent inside an open service window also became billable, while the 72-hour free entry point from Click-to-WhatsApp ads remains free. For commerce PMs, this changes the unit economics of support-heavy WhatsApp flows.
rationales: Correct. There's a monthly free allowance of 1,000 per number, after which service messages are billed.
There's still a free monthly allowance; charging starts after 1,000.
Businesses bear the charges; customers are not charged for receiving messages.
The 24-hour window remains; what changed is billing beyond the allowance.
questions.interview_tip: If you interview for commerce or messaging roles, connect platform pricing changes to unit economics and channel strategy (e.g., deflecting volume to self-serve or ad-driven free windows).
